content: Reports of adverse reactions in patients undergoing therapy with injectable gold (sodium aurothiomalate) in combination with ACE inhibitors, including Altace (ramipril), are rare. In elderly patients, those who are volume-depleted (such as individuals on diuretic therapy), or those with compromised renal function, the concurrent use of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), including selective cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) inhibitors, with ACE inhibitors like ramipril, may lead to a decline in renal function. This can include the development of acute renal failure. These effects are typically reversible. Renal function should be monitored periodically in patients receiving both ramipril and NSAID therapy. The antihypertensive effects of ACE inhibitors, including ramipril, may be diminished when used concurrently with NSAIDs. The use of aliskiren in combination with Altace is contraindicated in patients with diabetes. Additionally, the concomitant use of aliskiren with Altace should be avoided in patients with renal impairment. Patients receiving mTOR inhibitor therapy (e.g., temsirolimus) may have an increased risk of angioedema. Carcinogenicity studies in rats and mice, where ramipril was administered by gavage for up to 24 months in rats at doses up to 500 mg/kg/day and for up to 18 months in mice at doses up to 1000 mg/kg/day, showed no evidence of tumorigenic effects. These doses are approximately 200 times the maximum recommended human dose when adjusted for body surface area. Mutagenicity studies, including the Ames test in bacteria, the micronucleus test in mice, unscheduled DNA synthesis in a human cell line, and a forward gene-mutation assay in a Chinese hamster ovary cell line, revealed no mutagenic activity. Several metabolites and degradation products of ramipril also tested negative in the Ames test. Fertility studies in rats at doses as high as 500 mg/kg/day did not demonstrate any adverse effects on fertility. No teratogenic effects of ramipril were observed in studies conducted on pregnant rats, rabbits, and cynomolgus monkeys. The doses used in these studies were up to approximately 400 times (in rats and monkeys) and 2 times (in rabbits) the recommended human dose when adjusted for body surface area. Neither ramipril nor its metabolites have been found to interact with food, digoxin, antacids, furosemide, cimetidine, indomethacin, or simvastatin. Co-administration of ramipril and warfarin did not adversely affect the anticoagulant effects of warfarin. Similarly, co-administration of ramipril with phenprocoumon did not alter minimum phenprocoumon levels or interfere with the patients' anticoagulation status. Drugs that act on the renin-angiotensin system, such as Altace, are classified as Pregnancy Category D by the FDA. Their use during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy can impair fetal renal function and increase the risk of fetal and neonatal morbidity and mortality. Oligohydramnios, a potential consequence, may be associated with fetal lung hypoplasia and skeletal deformities. Neonatal adverse effects may include skull hypoplasia, anuria, hypotension, renal failure, and death. If pregnancy is detected, Altace should be discontinued as soon as possible. These adverse outcomes are generally associated with drug use during the second and third trimesters. Most epidemiologic studies examining fetal abnormalities after first-trimester exposure to antihypertensive drugs have not specifically distinguished drugs affecting the renin-angiotensin system from other antihypertensive agents.
